keySentence: Jo refused to let society define who she was.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: The world around Jo March had very clear ideas about what a young woman should want and be. She should want a husband and a home and should find satisfaction in managing both very well. Jo looked at this plan and felt something inside her that she could only describe as absolute refusal. She did not want to be unkind about it — she simply knew with great certainty it was not her life. She wanted to write and to travel and to think seriously and to be taken seriously by the world. Nothing society offered her matched what she actually needed and she would not pretend that it did. Jo refused to let society define who she was.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: The particular courage that Jo March demonstrated was not the dramatic kind that announces itself loudly. It was the quieter and more sustained courage of continuing to be herself in a world that found her inconvenient. Every social gathering she attended reminded her that her ambitions were considered slightly ridiculous by respectable people. Every rejection letter she received confirmed what polite society was already suggesting — that she was reaching too far. Jo absorbed these messages and continued reaching because she had no other honest option available to her. She could perform the conventional life and disappear inside it or she could refuse the performance and pay the social price. She chose to pay the price because the alternative was a kind of self-erasure she was constitutionally incapable of accepting. Jo refused to let society define who she was.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: Jo's refusal to be defined by society is presented in Little Women not as heroic defiance but as simple psychological necessity. Alcott avoids making Jo's unconventionality into a virtue in itself — it is simply the natural expression of who Jo actually is. This distinction matters because it separates Jo from the type of rebel who performs non-conformity as a social identity. Jo is not refusing convention to make a point or to be interesting or to attract a particular kind of admiration. She is refusing it because accepting it would require her to systematically misrepresent herself to everyone she knows. The cost of conformity for Jo is not inconvenience but inauthenticity — and inauthenticity, for Jo, is not livable. Alcott presents this not as unusual but as the natural condition of anyone whose inner life is sufficiently developed and strong. The question the novel implicitly poses is not why Jo refuses but why more people with equally strong inner lives do not. Jo refused to let society define who she was.
